section_summary: This section continues a survey of Japan’s postwar press, covering newsroom democratization, management resignations, labor disputes, Communist influence, editorial rights, newsprint allocation, and the distribution and circulation of major national and regional newspapers. It concludes with SCAP’s July 1948 removal of pre-publication censorship from leading newspapers and news agencies. A new article by Masao Tsuda then begins, recounting the formation of the All-Japan Press and Radio Workers Union and the early Yomiuri labor disputes.

subfiles.title: The Post-War Press
subfiles.about: A survey of the democratization, labor conflicts, economic conditions, geographic distribution, and censorship status of the Japanese press after World War II.
subfiles.summary: This continuation traces postwar democratization inside the Asahi, Mainichi, Yomiuri, and provincial newspaper offices, including executive resignations, labor struggles, Communist influence, and disputes over editorial authority. It describes government and industry arrangements for allocating scarce newsprint and the rapid but precarious growth of newly established newspapers. Detailed regional and institutional profiles provide circulation figures, affiliations, editorial tendencies, and collateral publications for leading national and provincial dailies. The report closes with SCAP's July 15, 1948 removal of pre-publication censorship from major newspapers and news agencies and an explanation of the resulting post-publication controls.

subfiles.title: Post-War Labor Movement Among Japanese Newspaper Workers
subfiles.about: Masao Tsuda recounts the creation of a nationwide Japanese press workers' union and the development of militant newspaper labor disputes after the surrender.
subfiles.summary: Tsuda: demands for accountability produced newspaper unions and the All-Japan Press and Radio Workers Union of February 9, 1946; its hurried formation and dependence on management; the Yomiuri disputes under Tomin Suzuki and Shoriki's weakening.
